Compare stage 1 with stage 4. Every token leaves the block with the same
number of dimensions but a larger norm (length) than it arrived with: norms
go from 1.03 to roughly 2.2–2.7. More importantly, every token leaves with
content it did not have. `kedi` entered as *animate*
and leaves as *animate, attached to an action*. That is one block. Stack
twelve and each one gets to condition on what the previous eleven worked out.

### Where the parameters actually live

The block has a fixed shape, so its size is a formula. With $d_{\text{ff}} =
4d$:

| part | matrices | parameters |
|:--|:--|--:|
| attention | $W^Q, W^K, W^V, W^O$, each $d \times d$ | $4d^2$ |
| feed-forward | $d \times 4d$ and $4d \times d$ | $8d^2$ |
| **block total** | | $\mathbf{12d^2}$ |

Biases and layer-norm parameters are $O(d)$ and round to nothing. So:

| $d_{\text{model}}$ | attention | feed-forward | one block |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 768 | 2,359,296 | 4,718,592 | 7,077,888 |
| 1,024 | 4,194,304 | 8,388,608 | 12,582,912 |
| 4,096 | 67,108,864 | 134,217,728 | 201,326,592 |
| 8,192 | 268,435,456 | 536,870,912 | 805,306,368 |

[Two thirds of every transformer *block* is the feed-forward half.]{.hl} People
say "attention is all you need" and then build blocks in which attention is a
third of the weights.

Say *block*, not *model*. The ratio holds inside a block; across a whole model
the embeddings dilute it, and how much depends on the size. In GPT-2 small
below, the 12 blocks are only 68% of the parameters, so the feed-forward share
of the *model* is about 46%. At $d = 8192$ the embeddings are a rounding error
and the model ratio converges back on two thirds. Small models are mostly
vocabulary; large models are mostly feed-forward.

And two thirds is not a ceiling. It assumes the GPT-2 shape: $8d^2$ of
feed-forward against $4d^2$ of attention. A Llama-3 block moves in both
directions at once. Its SwiGLU feed-forward costs $10.5d^2$, and its attention
costs only $2.5d^2$ — grouped-query attention shrinks $W^K$ and $W^V$ from
$d \times d$ to $d \times 1024$ (@sec-attention-cost), so that pair costs
$0.5d^2$ instead of $2d^2$. The feed-forward share is therefore
$10.5/13 = \mathbf{81\%}$, not the 72% you get by assuming full-width
attention. Almost every architectural change of the last few years has moved
weight *into* this sublayer or *out of* attention, rarely the reverse.

A rule of thumb is only worth having if it reproduces a number you can look
up. GPT-2 small is public: vocabulary 50,257, $d = 768$, 12 layers, context
1,024.

| part | arithmetic | parameters |
|:--|:--|--:|
| token embeddings | $50{,}257 \times 768$ | 38,597,376 |
| position embeddings | $1{,}024 \times 768$ | 786,432 |
| 12 blocks | $12 \times 12 \times 768^2$ | 84,934,656 |
| **total** | | **124,318,464** |

The published size is ~124M, and the rule lands within **0.098%** of it. The
residual is not mysterious — it is exactly the $O(d)$ terms the rule throws
away. Restore them and the count closes completely:

| dropped term | arithmetic | parameters |
|:--|:--|--:|
| attention biases | $12 \times (3d + d)$ | 36,864 |
| feed-forward biases | $12 \times (4d + d)$ | 46,080 |
| layer-norm $\gamma, \beta$ | $12 \times 2 \times 2d + 2d$ | 38,400 |
| **exact total** | 124,318,464 + 121,344 | **124,439,808** |

So the rule is not an approximation with unexplained slop; it is an exact
count with three named terms deleted. Trust it for capacity planning, and
remember which terms you dropped when someone asks why your number and the
model card differ in the last five digits.

::: {.column-margin}
Notice what the table does *not* contain: an output projection back to the
vocabulary. GPT-2 ties the output weights to the input embedding matrix, so
those 38.6M parameters are counted once and used twice.
:::

## Positional information: absolute, learned, RoPE, ALiBi {#sec-position}

Because attention itself is order-blind, position must be injected
explicitly — the model literally cannot tell "dog bites man" from "man bites
dog" without it. This is the same failure the averaged embeddings hit in
@sec-bake-off, where `kalite iyi fiyat kötü` and `kalite kötü fiyat iyi`
came out at cosine 1.0000.

### First, prove the problem is real

That claim is easy to state and easy to believe without checking, so check
it. Take the worked example, shuffle the three tokens into the order `içti
kedi sütü`, run attention again, then un-shuffle the outputs and compare:

| token | outputs, original order | outputs, shuffled then un-shuffled |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `kedi` | `[0.7444, 0.3433]` | `[0.7444, 0.3433]` |
| `sütü` | `[0.3256, 0.7443]` | `[0.3256, 0.7443]` |
| `içti` | `[0.5308, 0.6009]` | `[0.5308, 0.6009]` |

Largest disagreement anywhere in the table: $1.11 \times 10^{-16}$, which is
floating-point noise and not a difference. [Unmasked self-attention is
*permutation equivariant*: shuffle the inputs and the outputs shuffle with
them, otherwise untouched.]{.hl}

This is not a bug that someone forgot to fix; it follows from the definition.
Every token's output is a weighted sum over all tokens, and a sum does not
care what order you add things in. Nothing anywhere in $QK^{\top}$, softmax,
or $AV$ can see an index. A bag of words with a very clever averaging scheme
is still a bag of words.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**"Unmasked" is doing real work in that sentence.** Add the causal mask of
@sec-model-families and the symmetry breaks: token 1 may attend to one position,
token 5 to five, so the *number of visible tokens* already encodes an index.
Decoder-only models can therefore learn position with no positional encoding
at all — the so-called **NoPE** result [@kazemnejad2023impact], which at small
scale even extrapolates to longer sequences better than some explicit schemes.
In practice everyone still adds an explicit signal, because a count is a weak
and indirect way to learn order. But the honest statement is that the mask
leaks position, not that a decoder is blind without an encoding.
:::

### Adding a position signal

The original Transformer's answer is to build a vector for each *slot* and add
it to whatever word lands there [@vaswani2017attention]. The vector is made of
sines and cosines at geometrically spaced frequencies:

$$
\text{PE}_{(\text{pos},\, 2i)} = \sin\!\left(\frac{\text{pos}}{10000^{2i/d}}\right),
\qquad
\text{PE}_{(\text{pos},\, 2i+1)} = \cos\!\left(\frac{\text{pos}}{10000^{2i/d}}\right)
$$

At $d = 4$ there are two frequencies — one fast, one a hundred times slower —
and the whole encoding fits in three rows:

| position | $\sin(\text{pos})$ | $\cos(\text{pos})$ | $\sin(\text{pos}/100)$ | $\cos(\text{pos}/100)$ |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 | 0.0000 | 1.0000 | 0.0000 | 1.0000 |
| 1 | 0.8415 | 0.5403 | 0.0100 | 1.0000 |
| 2 | 0.9093 | −0.4161 | 0.0200 | 0.9998 |

Add $0.3 \times \text{PE}$ to the embeddings and repeat the shuffle test.
[The subtlety that makes it work: when the words move, the position vectors do
**not** move with them.]{.hl} Position 0 is still position 0, so a word that
was first and is now third gets a different vector than before:

| token | outputs, original order | outputs, shuffled then un-shuffled |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `kedi` | `[0.8029, 0.7345]` | `[1.1319, 0.5094]` |
| `sütü` | `[0.6385, 1.0023]` | `[0.7489, 0.6805]` |
| `içti` | `[0.7865, 0.8342]` | `[0.8767, 0.6607]` |

Largest disagreement: **0.3289**. The order-blindness is gone.

::: {#gloss-positional-encoding .column-margin .term-gloss}
**positional encoding** — the position signal added to (or applied to) token embeddings, because attention alone is order-blind. [↩](#term-positional-encoding){.term-back}
:::

### Why sinusoids in particular

Any distinct vector per slot would break the tie. Sinusoids were chosen
because of a property that is easy to state and, unusually for this
literature, exactly true. For a [positional encoding](#gloss-positional-encoding){#term-positional-encoding .term-ref} built this way,

$$
\text{PE}_{p} \cdot \text{PE}_{p+k} \;=\; \sum_{i} \cos(k\,\omega_i)
$$

The $p$ terms cancel by the angle-difference identity, and what survives
depends only on $k$ — the *offset*. So the similarity between two positions is
a function of how far apart they are and not of where they sit in the
sequence.

If that were only approximately true it would be worth much less, so measure
it. Sweeping $p$ across 256 positions at $d = 64$ and holding the offset
fixed:

| offset $k$ | mean $\text{PE}_p \cdot \text{PE}_{p+k}$ | std over $p$ | range over $p$ |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 | 32.000000 | 1.6e−15 | 1.1e−14 |
| 1 | 30.916832 | 7.8e−15 | 4.6e−14 |
| 2 | 28.303862 | 1.1e−14 | 7.8e−14 |
| 4 | 23.934362 | 7.4e−15 | 5.0e−14 |
| 8 | 22.413912 | 5.8e−15 | 3.9e−14 |
| 16 | 19.372820 | 5.8e−15 | 3.9e−14 |
| 32 | 19.553972 | 1.0e−14 | 7.1e−14 |
| 64 | 13.906089 | 1.2e−14 | 9.1e−14 |

A standard deviation of $10^{-14}$ across 256 different absolute positions is
the identity holding exactly, in floating point. Every position vector also
has the same length, $\sqrt{d/2} = 5.656854$, to ten digits. That is a property
of the position vector, not of the sum: adding it changes the embedding's norm,
since $\lVert x + p \rVert^2 = \lVert x \rVert^2 + \lVert p \rVert^2 + 2\,x \cdot p$
depends on the angle between them. RoPE, further down, is the scheme that leaves
the norm alone.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Read the middle column honestly.** The mean is *not* monotonic in $k$: offset
32 scores higher than offset 16. It is a sum of cosines, so it wobbles. The
correct claim is "this quantity depends only on the offset", which the last
two columns establish beyond argument. The tempting claim — "nearby positions
look more similar than distant ones" — is not what the table shows, and a
textbook that says it anyway is asking you to trust a picture over the
numbers.
:::

::: {.anlp-widget}
```{=html}
<div class="widget-title">Sinusoidal position encodings, as a picture</div>
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof peDim = Inputs.range([8, 64], { step: 8, value: 32, label: "d_model" })
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof peN = Inputs.range([16, 128], { step: 16, value: 64, label: "positions" })
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
peGrid = {
  const out = [];
  for (let pos = 0; pos < peN; pos++)
    for (let i = 0; i < peDim / 2; i++) {
      const w = pos / Math.pow(10000, (2 * i) / peDim);
      out.push({ pos, dim: 2 * i, v: Math.sin(w) });
      out.push({ pos, dim: 2 * i + 1, v: Math.cos(w) });
    }
  return out;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  marginLeft: 46,
  height: 300,
  width: 680,
  x: { label: "position →", ticks: 8 },
  y: { label: "↑ dimension", reverse: true },
  color: { type: "diverging", scheme: "BuRd", domain: [-1, 1], legend: true },
  marks: [Plot.cell(peGrid, { x: "pos", y: "dim", fill: "v" })]
})
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"}
Low dimensions (top) flip sign every few positions; high dimensions (bottom)
barely change across the whole window. That spread of wavelengths is the
point — the fast dimensions encode "which neighbour", the slow ones encode
"roughly where in the document". Push `d_model` up and watch more slow
dimensions appear at the bottom.
:::
:::

### Learned absolute positions

Sinusoids are elegant and, as it turned out, unnecessary. BERT and GPT-2 both
threw them away and used an ordinary embedding table indexed by position: row
0 is the vector for slot 0, learned by gradient descent like any other
parameter [@devlin2019bert; @radford2019language]. It works about as well, and
you saw the cost in the parameter table above — GPT-2 small spends 786,432
parameters on it.

The real cost is elsewhere. [A learned table has exactly as many rows as you
trained it with.]{.hl} GPT-2's table has 1,024 rows, so token 1,025 has no
vector at all — not a degraded one, none. The context limit is not a tuning
choice you can relax at inference time; it is baked into the shape of a
weight matrix. Every "extend the context window" method for this family of
models is fundamentally about manufacturing rows that were never trained.

### RoPE: rotate instead of add

The dominant choice today is rotary position embedding, and its idea is a
genuine change of kind rather than a better table [@su2024roformer]. RoPE adds
nothing to the embedding. It takes the query and key vectors — after
projection, inside each head — splits them into consecutive pairs of
coordinates, and *rotates* each pair by an angle proportional to the position:

$$
\begin{bmatrix} q'_{2i} \\ q'_{2i+1} \end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix} \cos m\theta_i & -\sin m\theta_i \\
                \sin m\theta_i & \phantom{-}\cos m\theta_i \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} q_{2i} \\ q_{2i+1} \end{bmatrix},
\qquad \theta_i = 10000^{-2i/d_k}
$$

Here $m$ is the token's position and $d_k$ is the head dimension, since the
rotation happens inside each head. Rotating a vector by $m\theta$ and another by $n\theta$ and then taking their
dot product leaves an angle of $(m-n)\theta$. So the attention *score itself*
becomes a function of the offset — not a side channel added to the embedding
and hoped to survive the projections, but the score.

That is a strong claim, so here it is measured. One fixed random query and
key, $d = 64$, scored at a fixed offset from four wildly different absolute
positions ($n = 0, 100, 1000, 5000$):

| offset $m-n$ | score | spread across the four positions |
|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 | 2.152941 | 2.2e−15 |
| 1 | 3.606170 | 1.5e−13 |
| 2 | 5.453257 | 3.1e−13 |
| 5 | 6.457170 | 5.0e−13 |
| 10 | 8.827710 | 1.4e−13 |
| 50 | −0.061180 | 1.5e−13 |
| 200 | −13.740668 | 4.1e−14 |

Now the same measurement on the additive scheme, where the position vector is
summed into the embedding before projection:

| offset $m-n$ | score at $n=0$ | at $n=100$ | at $n=1000$ | spread over all four |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 | 31.19 | 26.98 | 48.15 | 26.3 |
| 1 | 31.82 | 27.54 | 47.52 | 26.6 |
| 10 | 13.74 | 20.55 | 38.85 | 25.1 |
| 200 | 1.86 | 6.43 | 25.00 | 23.1 |

Three of the four positions are printed; the spread column covers all four,
which is why the first two rows are wider than the visible columns alone would
give.

[A spread of $10^{-13}$ against a spread of 26.]{.hl} With addition, "five
tokens back" means something different at position 0 than at position 5,000,
and the model has to learn to cope with that. With rotation it means the same
thing everywhere, for free. RoPE also preserves vector norms exactly — a
rotation is a rotation — so it cannot distort the magnitude of a query the way
addition can.

This is why RoPE is in Llama, Qwen, Mistral, Gemma, and essentially every
open-weight model released since 2023, and why the main context-extension
tricks for those models (position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, YaRN) are
all reparameterisations of $\theta_i$ rather than new tables.

### ALiBi: skip the encoding, penalise distance

The most economical answer is to encode nothing and simply subtract a penalty
proportional to distance, directly on the attention scores [@press2022alibi]:

$$
\text{score}(i, j) = \frac{q_i \cdot k_j}{\sqrt{d_k}} - m\,(i - j)
$$

The penalty is subtracted *after* the $\sqrt{d_k}$ scaling, not before — which
matters, because it is what makes the slopes $m$ transferable across models of
different width.

Each head gets its own fixed slope $m$, on a geometric schedule. With eight
heads the slopes are $\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \dots, \tfrac{1}{256}$, so
the head with $m = 0.5$ has accumulated a penalty of 1 after 2 tokens (a
score lower by 1, which divides the attention weight by $e \approx 2.7$) and
is effectively local, while the head with $m = 1/256$ needs 256 tokens to
accumulate the same penalty and is effectively global. Different heads see
different distance scales, by construction.

The bias a head with $m = 0.5$ adds, over six tokens:

| | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **pos 0** | 0.0 | −∞ | −∞ | −∞ | −∞ | −∞ |
| **pos 1** | −0.5 | 0.0 | −∞ | −∞ | −∞ | −∞ |
| **pos 2** | −1.0 | −0.5 | 0.0 | −∞ | −∞ | −∞ |
| **pos 3** | −1.5 | −1.0 | −0.5 | 0.0 | −∞ | −∞ |
| **pos 4** | −2.0 | −1.5 | −1.0 | −0.5 | 0.0 | −∞ |
| **pos 5** | −2.5 | −2.0 | −1.5 | −1.0 | −0.5 | 0.0 |

That single matrix is the causal mask and the position signal at once, and it
contains no learned parameters whatsoever. Because it is defined by a formula
over $i - j$, it is defined for any distance, which is what lets an ALiBi
model trained at length 1,024 run at length 2,048 without falling over — the
result the paper's title advertises.

### Choosing

| scheme | how position enters | extra parameters | beyond training length |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| sinusoidal | added to embeddings | none | defined, but quality degrades |
| learned absolute | added to embeddings | $n_{\text{ctx}} \times d$ | **undefined** — no row exists |
| RoPE | rotates Q and K per head | none | defined, but degrades sharply; usable only after rescaling $\theta$ |
| ALiBi | subtracted from scores | none | degrades gracefully by design |

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**RoPE does not extrapolate on its own.** Because it is a formula over $i - j$,
RoPE is *defined* at any distance — but a model trained at 4k typically falls
apart well before 8k, because the rotation angles it sees past the training
length are ones it never encountered. That failure is exactly why the
long-context toolkit exists: **Position Interpolation** squeezes unseen
positions back into the trained range [@chen2023extending], and **NTK-aware
scaling** and **YaRN** [@peng2024yarn] rescale $\theta$ frequency-by-frequency
instead of uniformly. Every "extended to 128k" announcement about a RoPE model
is announcing one of these plus continued training — not a free property of
RoPE.
:::

[The column that matters in practice is the last one.]{.hl} When a vendor
announces a context window, they are describing a property of the position
scheme as much as of the training data — and when a model becomes strangely
unreliable past some length, the position scheme is the first place to look.
Advertised context length and *usable* context length are different numbers,
a gap we will measure rather than assume in @sec-context-engineering.

## Encoder-only, decoder-only, encoder-decoder {#sec-model-families}

Here is a fact that sounds like a simplification and mostly is not:
[the structural difference between BERT-style and GPT-style *self-attention* is
which entries of the attention matrix are allowed to be non-zero.]{.hl} Two
qualifications travel with it, and the rest of this section makes both: an
encoder–decoder is two stacks joined by cross-attention, which no mask over one
stack produces, and the names BERT and GPT also carry particular embeddings,
normalisation placements and training objectives.

Same blocks, same multi-head attention, same feed-forward sublayer, same
residual stream. What differs is a [causal mask](#gloss-causal-mask){#term-causal-mask .term-ref} applied to the scores before the
softmax — and, following from that, what the model can be trained to do.

::: {#gloss-causal-mask .column-margin .term-gloss}
**causal mask** — blocks every position from attending to later ones, so the model can be trained to generate left to right. [↩](#term-causal-mask){.term-back}
:::

### The mask is the architecture

Look at the three patterns.

::: {.anlp-widget}
```{=html}
<div class="widget-title">Which token may look at which</div>
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
mskToks = ["kedi", "sütü", "içti", "çünkü", "açtı"]
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof mskKind = Inputs.radio(
  ["bidirectional (encoder)", "causal (decoder)", "prefix (prefix-LM)"],
  { value: "causal (decoder)", label: "Mask" }
)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof mskPrefix = Inputs.range([1, 4], {
  step: 1, value: 2, label: "prefix length", disabled: !mskKind.startsWith("prefix")
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
mskCells = {
  const n = mskToks.length;
  const out = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (let j = 0; j < n; j++) {
      let ok;
      if (mskKind.startsWith("bidirectional")) ok = true;
      else if (mskKind.startsWith("causal")) ok = j <= i;
      else ok = i < mskPrefix ? j < mskPrefix : j <= i;
      out.push({ q: mskToks[i], k: mskToks[j], ok });
    }
  return out;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  marginLeft: 62,
  marginTop: 46,
  height: 280,
  width: 420,
  x: { domain: mskToks, label: "attended to (key) →", axis: "top", tickRotate: -30 },
  y: { domain: mskToks, label: "↓ attending (query)" },
  color: { domain: [true, false], range: ["#0E7C7B", "#E6E3DC"], legend: false },
  marks: [
    Plot.cell(mskCells, { x: "k", y: "q", fill: "ok", inset: 1.5 }),
    Plot.text(mskCells, {
      x: "k", y: "q", text: d => (d.ok ? "✓" : "·"),
      fill: d => (d.ok ? "white" : "currentColor"), fontSize: 13
    })
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<p style="margin:0.4rem 0 0;font-size:0.85rem;">${
  mskKind.startsWith("bidirectional")
    ? "Every token sees the whole sentence, including what comes after it. Excellent representations — and useless for generation, because predicting the next word is trivial when you can already see it."
    : mskKind.startsWith("causal")
    ? "Lower triangular, diagonal included. Token i sees only tokens 0…i, so \"predict the next one\" is an honest task at every position at once. This is the mask that makes pre-training on raw text work."
    : "The first " + mskPrefix + " tokens see each other in both directions; everything after is causal. Used when there is a fixed instruction or document to encode and a continuation to generate."
}</p>`
```
:::

Select the causal mask and the top-right triangle goes grey. `kedi`, in
position 0, can then attend only to itself. That constraint is the entire
reason a decoder can be trained on raw text: with it, the model can be asked
to predict *every* token in a sentence simultaneously without ever seeing the
answer, which turns one document into thousands of training signals.

Mechanically it is one line — set the masked scores to $-\infty$ before the
softmax, so $e^{-\infty} = 0$ and those tokens receive exactly zero weight.
Setting the weights to zero *after* the softmax would not be equivalent,
because the remaining weights would no longer sum to 1.

::: {.fig-cap}
Rows are queries, columns are keys, and the whole taxonomy of model families
reduces to which cells are switched on.
:::
::::

| family | mask | trained to | representative | good at |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| encoder-only | bidirectional | fill in masked tokens | BERT [@devlin2019bert] | classification, extraction, retrieval embeddings |
| decoder-only | causal | predict the next token | GPT, Llama, Qwen | generation, and — since scale — everything else |
| encoder-decoder | bidirectional in, causal out | produce a target sequence | T5 [@raffel2020exploring], BART | translation, summarization, any input→output rewrite |

An encoder-decoder needs one extra mechanism. Its decoder runs self-attention
over what it has generated so far, and then a second attention sublayer called
**cross-attention** in which [the queries come from the decoder while the keys
and values come from the encoder]{.hl}. It is the same arithmetic you worked
through above — the only change is that $Q$ and $K, V$ are computed from two
different sequences. With $m$ target tokens and $n$ source tokens, the score
matrix is $m \times n$ — no longer square. That is how "attend to the source
sentence while writing the translation" is expressed.

::: {.column-margin}
Cross-attention is also how most multimodal models attach an image to a
language model: the image encoder produces keys and values, the language model
supplies the queries. We come back to this in @sec-multimodal.
:::

### Why decoder-only won

In 2019 the sensible prediction was that each family would keep its niche.
That is not what happened; almost everything you will use in this book is
decoder-only. Three reasons, in rough order of importance.

**One objective, all the data.** Next-token prediction needs no labels, no
corruption scheme, and no paired data. Every document on the internet is
training data for it, and every position in that document is a training
example.

**Task-as-text.** Once a model is good enough at continuation, classification
and translation and summarization can all be *written down* as prompts rather
than built as separate heads. The architectural specialisation of an
encoder-decoder stops paying for itself when a general model can be asked
politely. This is the story of @sec-prompting.

**Cheap incremental decoding.** With a causal mask, the representation of
token $i$ never depends on anything after it — so when you append a token, all
the earlier work is still valid. That is what makes the KV cache possible, and
the KV cache is why generation costs what it costs.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Encoder-only models are not obsolete.** For classification and retrieval at
volume, a 110M-parameter BERT-style encoder is often 100× cheaper per document
than a generative model and just as accurate, because it emits one vector in
one forward pass instead of decoding token by token. Most of the embedding
models behind the retrieval systems in @sec-rag are encoders (a few recent ones
are decoders adapted to the job). Choosing a 7B decoder
for sentiment analysis is a common and expensive mistake — and @sec-bake-off
already showed how often the cheaper representation wins.
:::

## Efficiency: FlashAttention, GQA/MQA, KV cache {#sec-attention-cost}

Everything so far has been about what attention computes. This section is
about what it costs, which is the part that decides whether you can actually
run the thing.

### The quadratic term, in bytes

$QK^{\top}$ is $n \times n$. That is the whole problem in one line. Written
naively, a single head at a single layer must hold that matrix in memory. At
fp16 (16-bit floating point) each number takes 2 bytes; a GiB is $2^{30}$
bytes, about 1.07 GB:

| sequence length | entries in $QK^{\top}$ | one score matrix at fp16 |
|--:|--:|--:|
| 512 | 262,144 | 0.0005 GiB |
| 4,096 | 16,777,216 | 0.03 GiB |
| 32,768 | 1,073,741,824 | 2.00 GiB |
| 100,000 | 10,000,000,000 | 18.63 GiB |

[Eighteen gigabytes for one head at one layer.]{.hl} Multiply by 32 heads and
32 layers and the number stops being a memory problem and becomes a fantasy.

### When does attention actually dominate?

The quadratic term is not always the term that matters, and people routinely
overestimate it. Per layer, ignoring constants:

$$
\underbrace{24\,n\,d^2}_{\text{projections and FFN}}
\qquad\text{versus}\qquad
\underbrace{4\,n^2 d}_{\text{scores and weighting}}
$$

Setting them equal gives $n = 6d$. Below that, the transformer spends most of
its time on matrix multiplications that are perfectly ordinary and linear in
sequence length:

| $d_{\text{model}}$ | sequence length $n$ | | attention's share of FLOPs |
|--:|--:|:--|--:|
| 768 | 1,024 | | 18% |
| 768 | 4,608 | *crossover* | 50% |
| 768 | 32,768 | | 88% |
| 4,096 | 4,096 | | 14% |
| 4,096 | 24,576 | *crossover* | 50% |
| 4,096 | 100,000 | | 80% |

[At the context lengths most applications actually use, attention is a
*minority* of the compute.]{.hl} A 4,096-wide model running 4,096 tokens
spends 86% of its arithmetic on the feed-forward and projection matrices. The
quadratic term is a wall you hit at long context, not a tax you pay at every
length — and knowing which regime you are in tells you whether optimising
attention is worth any of your time.

### FlashAttention: don't build the matrix

Here is the observation that made long context practical: on a modern GPU,
attention is not limited by arithmetic. It is limited by moving that
$n \times n$ matrix between fast on-chip memory and slow high-bandwidth
memory. The FLOPs are cheap; the round trips are not [@dao2022flashattention].

FlashAttention therefore never materialises the score matrix. It walks through
the sequence in tiles, keeping a running softmax normaliser so that a
partially-computed softmax can be corrected as new tiles arrive, and
accumulates the output directly.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**FlashAttention is exact.** It is not a sparse approximation, a low-rank
factorisation, or a windowed heuristic. It computes the same function as the
naive implementation and differs only in what it stores. Exact is not the same
as *bit-identical*: the online softmax re-associates the sums, and
floating-point addition is not associative, so the last digits can move — the
same way any two matrix-multiply kernels disagree in the last digits. What you
never trade is quality, which is why it went from a paper to a default in
about eighteen months, and why memory use in attention is now linear in $n$
even though the computation is still quadratic.
:::

### The KV cache: the number that decides deployment

Generation is incremental. Having produced 500 tokens, the model produces the
501st — and because the mask is causal, the keys and values of the first 500
have not changed. Recomputing them would be pure waste, so they are kept. That
store is the [KV cache](#gloss-kv-cache){#term-kv-cache .term-ref}, and it converts generation from quadratic-per-token to
linear-per-token.

::: {#gloss-kv-cache .column-margin .term-gloss}
**KV cache** — stored keys and values from earlier tokens, so generation does not recompute them. Its size, not the model's, usually decides how many users a GPU can serve. [↩](#term-kv-cache){.term-back}
:::

This splits a request into two phases with very different characters. The
prompt is processed all at once, in parallel, exactly as in training, and its
keys and values fill the cache — this is called *prefill*. After that, each
new token is one small step (*decode*): little arithmetic per step, but all of
the model's weights and the whole cache must be read from memory for every
new token. That is why generation speed is usually limited by memory
bandwidth rather than by arithmetic, a point @sec-serving builds on.

With a cache, the keys and values of the first five tokens are read back from memory unchanged and only the sixth is computed. The saving in arithmetic is paid for in memory, which grows linearly with context length and is duplicated for every concurrent request.">

::: {.fig-cap}
The cache is the reason generation is affordable and the reason long context
is not. It trades $O(n)$ recomputation per step — $O(n^2)$ over a whole
generation — for $O(n)$ storage, held separately for every concurrent request.
:::
::::

It also eats your GPU:

$$
\text{bytes} = 2 \times L \times h_{\text{kv}} \times d_{\text{head}} \times
n_{\text{tokens}} \times \text{bytes per value}
$$

The leading 2 is for K and V. Note what is *absent*: the number of query
heads, and the model's parameter count. Note what is present: the number of
tokens, linearly, and **per concurrent request**.

| model shape | layers | KV heads | head dim | context | KV cache |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 7B-class | 32 | 32 | 128 | 4,096 | 2.1 GB |
| 7B-class | 32 | 32 | 128 | 32,768 | 17.2 GB |
| 70B-class, *hypothetical* MHA | 80 | 64 | 128 | 32,768 | 85.9 GB |
| 7B-class | 32 | 32 | 128 | 100,000 | 52.4 GB |

A 7B model in fp16 is 14 GB of weights. At 100,000 tokens of context its KV
cache is 52 GB — [nearly four times the model itself, for one
conversation.]{.hl} This is the arithmetic behind every "why is long context
so expensive?" question, and it is why serving systems care so much about how
that memory is partitioned and reused (@sec-serving).

The third row is marked *hypothetical* on purpose: **today's 70B-class models
do not have 64 KV heads.** The original LLaMA 65B still used full multi-head
attention, but Llama 2 70B, Llama 3, Mistral's models and their descendants use
8, and the next section explains why. Redo the
arithmetic with $h_{\text{kv}} = 8$ and the 85.9 GB becomes **10.7 GB**. That
one substitution is the difference between a model that needs a node and a
model that fits on a card, and it is the single most consequential number in
this chapter.

::: {.anlp-widget}
```{=html}
<div class="widget-title">KV cache calculator</div>
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof kvLayers = Inputs.range([8, 128], { step: 4, value: 32, label: "layers" })
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof kvQHeads = Inputs.range([8, 128], { step: 4, value: 32, label: "query heads" })
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof kvScheme = Inputs.radio(
  ["MHA (KV heads = query heads)", "GQA, 8 KV heads", "GQA, 4 KV heads", "MQA (1 KV head)"],
  { value: "MHA (KV heads = query heads)", label: "Scheme" }
)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof kvCtx = Inputs.range([1024, 200000], { step: 1024, value: 32768, label: "context tokens" })
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof kvBytes = Inputs.radio([2, 1], {
  value: 2, label: "bytes per value", format: b => (b === 2 ? "fp16 (2)" : "fp8 (1)")
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
kvHeads = kvScheme.startsWith("MHA") ? kvQHeads
  : kvScheme === "GQA, 8 KV heads" ? 8
  : kvScheme === "GQA, 4 KV heads" ? 4 : 1
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
kvTotal = 2 * kvLayers * kvHeads * 128 * kvCtx * kvBytes
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
kvBaseline = 2 * kvLayers * kvQHeads * 128 * kvCtx * 2
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<div style="font-size:0.9rem;line-height:1.7;">
  <div style="font-size:1.6rem;font-weight:600;">${(kvTotal / 1e9).toFixed(1)} GB</div>
  <div>head dim fixed at 128 · ${kvHeads} KV head${kvHeads === 1 ? "" : "s"} ·
  ${(kvTotal / kvCtx / 1e3).toFixed(1)} KB per token</div>
  <div style="margin-top:0.35rem;">
  ${kvTotal < kvBaseline
    ? `<strong>${(kvBaseline / kvTotal).toFixed(1)}× smaller</strong> than fp16 multi-head attention at the same shape (${(kvBaseline / 1e9).toFixed(1)} GB).`
    : "This is the multi-head fp16 baseline."}
  </div>
  <div style="margin-top:0.35rem;color:#8a8a8a;">
  For scale: one 80 GB accelerator holds
  ${Math.max(0, Math.floor(80e9 / kvTotal))} concurrent request${Math.floor(80e9 / kvTotal) === 1 ? "" : "s"} of this size,
  before leaving any room for the weights.
  </div>
</div>`
```
:::

### GQA and MQA: fewer keys, same queries

The formula has an obvious lever. Nothing requires every query head to have
its own key and value head — several query heads can share one set.

- **Multi-query attention** takes this to the limit: all query heads share a
  single K/V head [@shazeer2019fast].
- **Grouped-query attention** is the compromise that won: query heads are
  divided into groups, one K/V head per group [@ainslie2023gqa].

On the 32-layer, 32-head, 100,000-token model above:

| scheme | KV heads | KV cache | reduction |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| MHA | 32 | 52.4 GB | 1× |
| GQA | 8 | 13.1 GB | **4×** |
| MQA | 1 | 1.6 GB | **32×** |

MQA's 32× is tempting and slightly too aggressive — quality degrades and
training gets unstable. GQA with 4 or 8 groups recovers essentially all the
quality for most of the saving, which is why Llama 2 70B, Llama 3, Mistral,
and nearly everything since ship with it. [It is a rare case where the
efficiency trick has almost no accuracy cost, which is exactly why it became
universal.]{.hl}

Notice, finally, that this is a decision you inherit rather than tune. You
cannot flip an MHA checkpoint to GQA in your serving config. You *can* convert
one — the GQA paper's own recipe mean-pools the key and value heads of each
group and then **uptrains** on roughly 5% of the original pretraining compute
[@ainslie2023gqa] — but 5% of a pretraining run is still a training run, with a
cluster and a budget and a week. For every practical purpose, "how big is the
KV cache" belongs in your model-selection checklist, not in your optimisation
backlog.

## Mixture of Experts {#sec-moe}

Two thirds of every transformer block is the feed-forward sublayer, and every
token goes through all of it. A [mixture of experts](#gloss-mixture-of-experts){#term-mixture-of-experts .term-ref} asks whether it has to.

Replace the single feed-forward network in a block with $E$ copies — the
*experts* — plus a small learned **router** that scores the experts for each
token and sends it to the best $k$ — $k = 2$ in the example below, $k = 8$
in many recent models. Only those $k$ run. The
other $E - k$ sit idle for that token, and a different token in the same
sentence may take a different pair.

::: {#gloss-mixture-of-experts .column-margin .term-gloss}
**mixture of experts** — replaces one feed-forward network with many, routing each token to a few of them, so total parameters and per-token compute stop being the same number. [↩](#term-mixture-of-experts){.term-back}
:::

::: {.fig-cap}
The router is a small learned layer that scores the experts and normalises the
top $k$. Six of the eight boxes do no arithmetic for this token — but all eight
still occupy memory.
:::
::::

[This severs a link that had held since the beginning: total parameters and
per-token compute stop being the same number.]{.hl} Take $d = 4096$, 32
layers, 8 experts, top-2 routing:

| | total parameters | active per token |
|:--|--:|--:|
| dense | 6.4B | 6.4B |
| MoE, 8 experts, top-2 | **36.5B** | **10.7B** |

The MoE model holds 5.7× the parameters of the dense one and does 1.67× the
arithmetic. Its memory bill follows the first number; the second is a
first-order estimate of the per-token arithmetic, not a latency figure. What you
actually wait for also depends on how evenly the routing spreads across experts,
on the communication that spreading costs, and on batch size and bandwidth.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**You rent the GPU for the total and get the latency of the active.** All 36.5B
parameters must be resident — the router's choice is per token, so any expert
may be needed at any moment. A "small active parameter count" in a launch post
tells you about speed, not about what you need to buy. This is the single
most misread number in open-weight model announcements, and it matters
directly when you cost out self-hosting in @sec-serving.
:::

The idea is old [@shazeer2017outrageously] and became practical when the
routing was simplified to one expert per token and the engineering worked out
at scale [@fedus2022switch]. The hard part in practice is not the routing rule
but **load balancing**: nothing stops the router from sending almost every
token to the same few experts and starving the rest, which wastes the parameters you paid for
and can collapse training.

The router itself is a single matrix. For token $x$ it produces
$s = xW_r \in \mathbb{R}^{E}$, keeps the top $k$ scores, renormalises them, and
mixes only those experts:

$$
\operatorname{MoE}(x) = \sum_{e \,\in\, \operatorname{top-}k(s)} \tilde g_e\, E_e(x),
\qquad \tilde g_e = \frac{\exp s_e}{\sum_{e' \in \operatorname{top-}k(s)} \exp s_{e'}}
$$

The classical fix for load balancing is an auxiliary loss penalising uneven
usage — an explicit correction for a failure mode the main objective is happy
to walk into. But it is a second objective fighting the first, and by 2025 the
largest open MoEs had demoted it: DeepSeek-V3 balances mainly with a per-expert
bias added to the routing score and adjusted online, carrying no gradient of its
own. "Mainly" is the operative word — it keeps a small complementary
sequence-wise balancing loss alongside that mechanism. Check which mechanism a
model actually uses, and in what proportion, rather than assuming the auxiliary
loss is either present or gone.

The 29% active fraction in the table above is a property of *this*
configuration, not of MoE. The direction the field went is **finer
granularity**: instead of 8 large experts with top-2, use 64–256 narrow experts
with top-8, plus one or two shared experts that every token visits. Same total,
far smaller active fraction — which is how a 35B-total model ends up near 3B
active rather than 10.7B, as `qwen3.6:35b-a3b` does in @sec-classification.
When you read a launch post, the ratio to look for is active over total, and
across shipped models it has ranged from about 30% down to 3%.

## Scaling laws and what they predict {#sec-scaling-laws}

Transformers turned out to have a property that almost nothing else in machine
learning has: [make them bigger and their loss falls in a way you can predict
in advance.]{.hl} Loss follows a power law in parameters, in data, and in
compute — a straight line on log-log axes over many orders of magnitude
[@kaplan2020scaling]. That predictability is the reason anyone was willing to
spend nine figures on a training run.

The first version of the analysis suggested growing the model much faster than
the data. It was wrong, in a way that matters and that is worth understanding
because the error was methodological rather than arithmetical: every run used
the same learning-rate schedule, whatever its number of training tokens. The
loss at smaller token counts was therefore read off runs whose schedule had
not finished, and it looked worse than a properly scheduled run would have
been. Redoing it properly gave a different
answer — [for a fixed compute budget, parameters and tokens should grow at
roughly the same rate]{.hl}, about 20 tokens per parameter
[@hoffmann2022chinchilla]:

| model | parameters | training tokens | tokens per parameter |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Gopher | 280B | 300B | 1.1 |
| Chinchilla | 70B | 1.4T | 20 |

Chinchilla is a quarter of Gopher's size, used the same compute budget, and
beat it broadly. A generation of models had been badly undertrained, and
nobody knew because everyone was reading the same scaling law.

Two honest qualifications, both of which you will need.

**The laws predict loss, not capability.** Loss is average negative
log-likelihood on held-out text. It is smooth and it is not what you care
about. Whether a model can follow a multi-step instruction, or refuse a bad
request, or do arithmetic reliably, is not a quantity these curves forecast —
and the relationship between a smooth loss curve and a jagged capability curve
remains genuinely disputed. Do not let a scaling plot tell you a model will be
able to do your task.

**Compute-optimal is not deployment-optimal.** Chinchilla optimises training
compute for a given loss. If you are going to serve a model to millions of
users, inference cost dominates its lifetime bill, and it is rational to train
a *smaller* model on far more tokens than the law recommends — paying more up
front to pay less forever. This is exactly what the Llama-family models do,
and why "trained past Chinchilla-optimal" is a design decision rather than a
mistake. We return to the full training pipeline in @sec-pretraining.

## Lab: implement attention, then profile it {#sec-attention-lab}

The point of this lab is to feel the quadratic term rather than read about it.
Work in NumPy first; reach for a framework only in step 3.

1. **Implement scaled dot-product attention** from the equation in
   @sec-attention-worked — projections, scores, scaling, optional mask,
   softmax, weighted sum. Write your own softmax and subtract the row maximum
   before exponentiating. No attention library.
2. **Reproduce this chapter's numbers exactly.** Use the same $E$, $W^Q$,
   $W^K$, $W^V$, and check that `içti`'s attention row comes out
   `[0.4230, 0.5012, 0.0759]`. If it does not, your bug is in the transpose or
   in the axis you are normalising over — those are the only two candidates.
3. **Verify against a reference.** Compare to
   `torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention` on random inputs at
   several shapes and report the maximum absolute difference. Anything above
   about $10^{-5}$ in fp32 is a real disagreement, not rounding.
4. **Confirm permutation equivariance.** With *no* mask, shuffle the tokens,
   run again, un-shuffle the outputs, and report the maximum difference. You
   should get machine epsilon, as this chapter did. Then add a positional
   encoding and report the number again. Finally repeat the whole test with a
   causal mask and no positional encoding: equivariance breaks even though you
   added no position signal. Explain why to someone who has not read this
   chapter.
5. **Measure the exponent.** Time attention at $n = 128, 256, \dots, 4096$
   with $d = 64$, holding everything else fixed. Plot on log-log axes and fit
   a slope. State what exponent you measured and whether it is 2 — and if it
   is well below 2 at small $n$, explain which fixed costs are hiding it.
6. **Measure the memory.** Instrument the peak size of the score matrix and
   compare it against the table in @sec-attention-cost. Find the $n$ at which
   your machine refuses. Report it.
7. **Add a causal mask**, then prove it works behaviourally rather than by
   inspection: run on a sequence, append one token, run again, and confirm
   the outputs for the original positions are unchanged. This invariant is
   what makes the next step legal.
8. **Build a KV cache.** Generate 512 tokens one at a time, first recomputing
   everything each step, then caching K and V. Plot per-token latency for both
   and report the speedup at token 512. Compute the cache's size in bytes from
   the formula in @sec-attention-cost and check it against what your process
   actually allocated.

**Deliverable:** the log-log plot with your fitted exponent, the two per-token
latency curves, and a short note on the largest sequence length your hardware
could handle — with the specific resource that ran out named.

## Intuition checks {#sec-transformers-intuition}

Answer each before you open it. These are the six places where the standard
mental model of a transformer is wrong in a way that costs money.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Attention is quadratic, so it dominates the cost of running a transformer. True?

Usually false, and believing it sends you optimising the wrong thing.

Per layer the two terms are $24nd^2$ for the projections and feed-forward
against $4n^2d$ for attention. They are equal at $n = 6d$ — so for a
4,096-wide model the crossover is at **24,576 tokens**. At the 4,096-token
context most applications actually run, [attention is 14% of the arithmetic
and the feed-forward and projection matrices are 86%]{.hl}.

The quadratic term is a wall you hit at long context, not a tax you pay at
every length. Before optimising attention, work out which regime you are in;
if $n < 6d$ you should be looking at the feed-forward half instead.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. If Q, K and V all come from the same input, why not use one matrix instead of three?

Because they answer three different questions, and collapsing them removes the
model's ability to ask.

$Q$ is what a token is looking *for*; $K$ is what it offers to be found *by*;
$V$ is what it actually contributes once found. [$Q$ and $K$ together decide
**where** information moves; $V$ alone decides **what** moves.]{.hl} Tie them
and a token's advert becomes identical to its query, so the score table is
forced to be a symmetric Gram matrix (a table of all pairwise dot products). Row normalisation can still produce
different weights in the two directions; what a head loses is the ability to
*choose* them, since both directions read one entry. It also biases every token toward itself, since $x \cdot x$ is
the largest score in a row unless a neighbour is longer; that second effect is
a tendency, not a guarantee.

The worked example in @sec-attention-worked shows this concretely: the score
that makes the example work could not have been produced by any unprojected
dot product of the inputs.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Your model has 100,000 tokens of context. What is the first resource to run out?

Memory, and not the model's. A 7B model in fp16 is 14 GB of weights. Its KV
cache at 100,000 tokens is **52.4 GB** — [nearly four times the model itself,
for one conversation]{.hl} — and that figure is *per concurrent request*,
while the weights are shared across all of them.

This is why the KV cache, not the parameter count, usually decides how many
users a GPU can serve, and why GQA became universal: dropping from 32 KV heads
to 8 takes the same cache from 52.4 GB to **13.1 GB**, a 4× saving with
essentially no quality cost.

If you answered "the $n \times n$ score matrix", that was the right answer
before FlashAttention, which never materialises it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. A mixture-of-experts model has 35B parameters. How much GPU memory do you need, and how fast is it?

Those are two different questions with two different answers, which is the
entire point of the architecture.

You must hold **all** 35B parameters in memory, because any token might route
to any expert. But only the top-$k$ experts run per token — about 3B active —
so latency tracks the small number. [Total parameters set your hardware bill;
active parameters set your latency.]{.hl}

@sec-classification-crossover measured exactly this: `qwen3.6:35b-a3b`
classifies a document in 0.353 s against 0.365 s for a *dense* 9.7B model and
0.592 s for a dense 27.4B — faster than both, while scoring higher than both,
and needing 23.9 GB on disk to do it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. Your model was trained with 1,024-position embeddings. What happens at token 1,025?

With learned absolute positions, nothing good: there is no row 1,025 in the
table, so the model has no vector to add. GPT-2 cannot process a longer
sequence at all — the failure is a lookup error, not a degradation.

This is the concrete reason the field moved to RoPE and ALiBi. RoPE encodes
position as a *rotation*, so the score between two tokens depends only on
their offset. Measured in @sec-position: the same query-key pair at a fixed
offset, evaluated at absolute positions 0, 100, 1000 and 5000, gives scores
that vary by at most **$5 \times 10^{-13}$** — against a spread of about 26
when the position vector is added to the embedding instead. [When position enters only as an offset, there is no row 1,025 to be
missing.]{.hl}

Note what this does *not* buy: extrapolating far beyond the training length
still degrades quality. It removes a hard failure and replaces it with a soft
one.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. Why does the residual stream matter more than any individual sublayer?

Because it is the only thing every sublayer reads from and writes to, and its
width never changes.

Attention and the feed-forward network both take the residual stream in and
add a correction back. That is why [stacking blocks is trivial — block 12
looks exactly like block 1]{.hl} — and it is why pre-norm normalises the
residual sum rather than the sublayer output.

The practical consequence: when you inspect what a transformer "knows" at some
depth, you are reading the residual stream, not any one layer's output. So does
every technique that extracts a vector from a mid-network layer — including the
frozen-encoder embeddings @sec-classification-finetune compares against.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-transformers-interview}

Transformer questions in interviews are usually a test of whether you can do
arithmetic about a system, not whether you can recite an architecture diagram.
The answers below are the ones with numbers attached.

::: {.column-margin}
If you get asked to "explain attention", resist the temptation to start with
the softmax formula. Start with what it is *for* — every token can look at
every other token and learn how much each one matters — then derive the
formula. Interviewers are listening for whether you understand it or memorised
it, and the order gives you away.
:::

1. **Explain self-attention to someone who knows regression.** It is a learned
   weighted average. Each token proposes a query, every token advertises a key,
   the dot products become weights through a softmax, and the output is those
   weights applied to the values. The only unusual part is that the weights are
   *computed from the data at inference time* rather than fitted once — which is
   exactly what makes the same word get a different vector in a different
   sentence. Then name the scaling: divide by $\sqrt{d_k}$, because dot products
   of $d_k$-dimensional vectors grow like $\sqrt{d_k}$ and an unscaled softmax
   saturates.

2. **Why is there a feed-forward network after attention?** Because attention
   mixes tokens but, given its weights, does so *linearly in the values* — the
   non-linearity it does have lives in how the weights are computed, not in what
   it does with what it moves. The feed-forward sublayer is where each token
   gets non-linear processing of its own: $W_1$ is a bank of detectors and
   $W_2$ is what each detector broadcasts when it fires. Get the proportion right, because most candidates
   have it backwards: in the standard $d_{\text{ff}} = 4d$ block used
   throughout this chapter, [two thirds of a transformer block's parameters are
   the feed-forward sublayer]{.hl}, not attention. The ratio follows from that
   choice of $d_{\text{ff}}$, so check it before quoting it elsewhere.

3. **How do you estimate whether a model fits on your GPU?** Two numbers, added.
   Weights: parameters × bytes per parameter (7B at fp16 = 14 GB). KV cache:
   $2 \times \text{layers} \times \text{KV heads} \times \text{head dim} \times
   \text{tokens} \times \text{bytes}$, **per concurrent request**. Give the
   worked case: a 7B model at 32,768 tokens needs 14 GB of weights and 17.2 GB
   of cache, so context has already cost more than the model. The senior version
   of the answer names the lever — GQA, quantisation, or a shorter context — and
   says which one you would pull first.

4. **What does FlashAttention actually change?** Not the mathematics: it computes the same function, and only the last digits move, because the tiled sums re-associate floating-point addition. It changes *what gets written to memory*: the $n \times
   n$ score matrix is never materialised, computed instead in tiles that stay in
   fast on-chip memory. That turns attention from memory-bandwidth-bound to
   compute-bound. The number that motivates it: at 100,000 tokens one score
   matrix for **one head at one layer** is 18.63 GiB in fp16. Multiply by 32
   heads and 32 layers and the naive version is not slow, it is impossible.

5. **Encoder-only, decoder-only, or encoder-decoder?** Inside self-attention
   the distinction is which entries of the attention matrix are allowed to be
   non-zero; an encoder-decoder adds cross-attention between two stacks.
   Encoder-only sees everything both ways and is the right choice when you need
   a representation of a complete text — classification, retrieval, and every
   result in @sec-classification. Decoder-only is causally masked and is what
   you need to generate. Encoder-decoder keeps both and lets the decoder attend
   to the encoder, which is why it persists in translation. Say the practical
   version: [for classification with labels, an encoder is still the default in
   2026]{.hl}, and @sec-classification-crossover has the measurement.

6. **Why did transformers replace RNNs?** Not because they are more expressive —
   because they are parallelisable in training. An RNN must process token $t$
   before token $t+1$; a transformer computes all positions at once, which
   converts a sequential dependency into a matrix multiplication and lets you
   use a GPU properly. The cost is the quadratic term and the loss of unbounded
   context. Be precise that this was an *engineering* win that unlocked scale,
   and that scale is what produced the capabilities — the argument
   @sec-scaling-laws makes quantitatively.

## Where to go deeper

Three outside visualizations pair beautifully with this chapter: the
[Illustrated Transformer](https://jalammar.github.io/illustrated-transformer/)
for step-by-step diagrams, Georgia Tech's
[Transformer Explainer](https://poloclub.github.io/transformer-explainer/),
which runs a live GPT-2 in your browser, and Brendan Bycroft's
[3D LLM walkthrough](https://bbycroft.net/llm).

If you would rather watch, three do this chapter better than any text:
3Blue1Brown's [Transformers, the tech behind LLMs](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wjZofJX0v4M)
and [Attention, step-by-step](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eMlx5fFNoYc)
for the geometry, Karpathy's
[Let's build GPT: from scratch](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kCc8FmEb1nY)
for the same architecture typed out line by line, and — if that pace is too
fast — Umar Jamil's slower
[Coding a Transformer from scratch in PyTorch](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ISNdQcPhsts),
which includes training and inference. Stanford's
[CS25: Transformers United](https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs25/) is a seminar
series where the authors present their own papers.

The primary sources are unusually readable, and after this chapter you have
enough to read them directly. Start with @vaswani2017attention — it is eight
pages and you now know every equation in it. Then, roughly in the order the
chapter needed them:

| topic | paper |
|:--|:--|
| the architecture | @vaswani2017attention |
| residual connections | @he2016deep |
| layer norm, and moving it | @ba2016layer; @xiong2020layernorm |
| what heads actually learn | @clark2019bert; @michel2019sixteen |
| rotary positions | @su2024roformer |
| position by distance penalty | @press2022alibi |
| exact, IO-aware attention | @dao2022flashattention |
| shrinking the KV cache | @shazeer2019fast; @ainslie2023gqa |
| sparse experts | @shazeer2017outrageously; @fedus2022switch |
| scaling laws, and their correction | @kaplan2020scaling; @hoffmann2022chinchilla |

If you want one book that derives the whole stack with runnable code rather
than a reading list, *Dive into Deep Learning* [@zhang2023dive] is free online
and covers attention and transformers from the linear algebra up.

## Exercises

1. In the attention explorer, the pronoun head splits its weight roughly
   46/34 between *coffee* and *robot* — leaning to the coffee, but only just.
   Write **three** one-word substitutions for *ready* that should push the
   ratio decisively one way or the other, and for each one state the fact
   about the world, not about grammar, that forces the reading. Then say what
   this implies about how much of a language model's competence can come from
   the attention pattern alone.
2. Attention is order-blind on its own. Take the word-order pair from
   @sec-bake-off that scored cosine 1.0000 under averaging, and explain
   precisely which component of a transformer block makes the two sentences
   representable differently.
3. A model with 32 layers, 32 heads, and head dimension 128 serves a 100,000
   token context. Compute the size of the KV cache in gigabytes at 16-bit
   precision. Then explain why grouped-query attention exists.
4. In the worked example, the fourth embedding dimension is 0.5 for all three
   tokens and it contributed nothing to any attention weight. Work out how far
   that generalises, in two parts. **(a)** Prove that the *key* side always
   cancels: show that whatever row $W^K$ assigns to a constant feature, its
   contribution is the same for every key $j$ and therefore vanishes in the
   softmax. **(b)** Then show by counterexample that the *query* side does
   not. Give $W^Q$ a non-zero row for the constant feature, recompute `içti`'s
   attention weights, and report how far they moved. Explain in one sentence
   why the same feature can matter in one projection and not the other.
5. Set $W^Q$ and $W^K$ back to a scale whose product is 1 instead of 3 and
   recompute `içti`'s attention row. Report the weights, and explain what the
   $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ term is protecting against in terms of what you observe.
6. The chapter claims $h$ heads of width $d/h$ cost the same as one head of
   width $d$. Verify this by counting parameters and multiplications for
   $d = 512$ at $h = 1, 8, 64$. Then state what is genuinely lost as $h$ grows,
   and at what point you would expect it to hurt.
7. Take the relative-position table for sinusoidal encodings. The mean at
   offset 32 is *higher* than at offset 16. Explain why from the formula
   $\sum_i \cos(k\omega_i)$, and say what this means for the common claim that
   sinusoidal encodings make nearby positions more similar.
8. Reproduce the RoPE experiment: one fixed random query and key, scored at
   offset 5 from absolute positions 0, 100, 1,000 and 5,000. Report the spread.
   Then do it with a learned-style additive encoding and report that spread.
   Use the two numbers to argue for or against RoPE in one paragraph.
9. A 70B-class model has 80 layers, 64 query heads, and head dimension 128.
   Its fp16 weights are 140 GB, so it is served on a node of four 80 GB
   accelerators — 320 GB total. Using the KV cache calculator, find the
   longest context you can serve to four concurrent users, first with 64 KV
   heads and then with 8, as current 70B-class models have. Report both
   lengths and the ratio between them. Then name every quantity in the cache
   formula that changed and every one that did not.
10. An announcement describes a model as "120B total parameters, 5B active".
    A colleague concludes it will run on a 24 GB consumer GPU because 5B is
    small. Write the two-sentence correction, with the arithmetic.
11. Gopher used 1.1 tokens per parameter and Chinchilla used 20. Both claims
    came from a scaling-law analysis. Explain what changed between them, and
    state what you would need to see in a new scaling-law paper before you
    reallocated a training budget on the strength of it.
